what_it_does: Large language models (LLMs) store their weights using very small numbers (4-bit integers, or 'INT4') to save memory, but the conversion from those tiny numbers back to working precision during computation adds 20-90% overhead that wipes out the savings. QServe introduces a combined algorithm-and-software approach called QoQ that uses 4-bit weights, 8-bit activations, and 4-bit memory for the model's running notes (the key-value cache), achieving up to 3.5x higher throughput than the industry-standard serving system on the same hardware.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A GPU has two kinds of arithmetic units: slow general-purpose CUDA cores and fast specialized tensor cores (the GPU's built-in matrix-multiply units, which are around 50x faster). Previous 4-bit quantization schemes forced expensive conversion work onto CUDA cores inside the innermost computation loop, completely hiding the speed advantage. QServe avoids this trap with three interlocking tricks.

Progressive quantization. Instead of going straight from full-precision weights to 4-bit, QServe compresses in two steps: first to 8-bit using a per-channel scale, then to 4-bit using a per-group scale. The first step is carefully constrained to the range [-119, 119] rather than the full 8-bit range of [-128, 127]. That narrow 'protective range' guarantees that when the 4-bit values are later expanded back to 8-bit during computation, they never overflow. Because overflow is impossible, a 4-way parallel addition instruction (vadd4) can process four weights simultaneously in a single clock, keeping all the work on fast tensor cores instead of slow CUDA cores.

Compute-aware weight reordering. Tensor cores need data in a strided layout — thread 0 needs elements 0-3 and 16-19, not a contiguous block. For 8-bit weights a hardware instruction handles this automatically, but for 4-bit weights it fails. QServe fixes this offline, before serving ever begins: it permanently reorders the stored weights into exactly the order each thread will consume them. This eliminates pointer arithmetic at runtime and allows 128-bit-wide memory reads, maximizing memory bandwidth.

SmoothAttention for 4-bit KV cache. The model's running notes (keys and values) have a few channels with values 10x larger than the rest, making 4-bit rounding inaccurate. QServe scales down those outlier channels before storage and absorbs that scale into the preceding layer's weights — a one-time offline change with no runtime cost. Bit tricks then reduce the arithmetic needed to unpack a 4-bit KV value from 5 operations to 2, and all attention math is moved from 32-bit CUDA cores to 16-bit tensor cores.

The result. On A100 and L40S GPUs, QServe achieves 1.2-3.5x higher throughput than TensorRT-LLM, the leading industry baseline, while maintaining accuracy within 0.2 perplexity points of the full-precision model.
